svg.title: Quantum computing impact on modern cryptography
svg.desc: Two panels, both contingent on a future cryptographically relevant quantum computer, none of which exists today. Public-key primitives face Shor's algorithm, which solves discrete logarithms and prime factorization in polynomial time and would break RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, and ECDH once run on such a machine, enabling retrospective decryption of recorded traffic; the migration action is FIPS 203 ML-KEM and FIPS 204 ML-DSA. Symmetric ciphers and hashes face Grover's algorithm, whose ideal sequential query bound is about 2 to the n over 2 — a query bound rather than a concrete wall-clock or practical strength rating. AES-128 remains NIST's Category 1 baseline and AES-256 adds margin.
svg.text: Quantum Computing Impact on Modern Cryptography
Contingent on a future Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) — none exists today
• Solves discrete logs & prime factorization efficiently
• Would break RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, & ECDH, once run on a CRQC
• Enables retrospective decryption of recorded TLS traffic
NOT YET BROKEN: Migrate Ahead of CRQC Arrival
• Quadratic speedup for unstructured brute-force search
• Not a concrete wall-clock or practical strength rating
• AES-128 is NIST Category 1; AES-256 adds margin
RETAIN AES; SELECT SIZE BY PROFILE AND RISK
Prioritize public-key migration by exposure lifetime; treat Grover exponents as query bounds, not concrete attack budgets.
